name: Orca Engine
description: Server-side intelligence engine for the Orca X TV app: personalization, recommendations, caching, and centralized administration.
overview: The brain/backbone for the Orca X Android TV client.

versions.changelog: Trailers can now come from more than one place. Until now TMDB was the only source, and a title TMDB had no video for simply had no trailer. There are now four sources, tried in an order you control from the Observatory's new Trailers settings group: tmdb (TMDB's videos, language-aware, as before), jellyfin (the trailer URLs Jellyfin's own metadata providers already found for a library item - free, no API key, and already on disk), stored (the URL saved on the catalog row), and search (ask yt-dlp to search YouTube by title and year). Removing a source from the list disables it; reordering changes preference. Search is off by default on purpose, because a text search can return a fan edit or a review and a confidently wrong trailer is worse than none. Three new controls decide which videos are acceptable at all: whether a teaser may stand in when no full trailer exists, whether only videos TMDB marks official are eligible, and whether non-YouTube videos such as Vimeo may be used - each narrows the field without changing the preference order, which still puts a trailer in your language above an official badge. The Trailer Resolver page gains a breakdown of which source actually answered and which were asked and came back empty, so a missing trailer now shows where the search stopped. Note this covers trailer URLs specifically; artwork and overviews still come from TMDB and Jellyfin alone.

The Observatory can now configure the engine, not just observe it. Its Settings page carries every admin setting the plugin has - the kill switch and home shape, all fifteen row feature flags, discovery tuning, the nine ranking weights, TMDB, Jellyseerr, Sonarr and Radarr credentials, the LLM provider and its three AI features, and all six embedding providers - grouped and explained, with the maintenance operations and counter reset alongside them. Changes are tracked as you make them: the bar at the top names exactly which settings are unsaved, Save writes them, and Discard puts them back. API keys are masked until you choose to reveal them. Reading and writing goes through Jellyfin's own plugin configuration API, so the Observatory and the plugin's page under Dashboard - Plugins are two views of the same stored settings and cannot disagree. Three settings that previously had no interface at all - the Spotlight showcase count and its feature flag, and the LLM discovery history cap - are editable for the first time, and any setting added to the engine in future appears automatically under Other settings rather than becoming unreachable. The plugin's existing configuration page is unchanged and still works.

Makes the Observatory easy to reach. It is now answered at the short address /orca - so on a typical setup, http://your-server:8096/orca rather than the full route - and there are two ways to it from inside Jellyfin that do not involve remembering any address at all: an Orca Observatory entry in the Jellyfin sidebar, and an Open Orca Observatory button on the plugin's own settings page under Dashboard - Plugins - Orca Engine, which also prints the direct link for bookmarking. The sidebar entry is only a redirect to the dashboard, not the dashboard itself: it renders its link as ordinary markup and merely enhances it with an automatic redirect, so it still works if its script does not run. The dashboard continues to run as its own standalone page. No engine behaviour, configuration or database changes.

Hardens the Observatory's status endpoint so it cannot fail as a whole. Each reading - process memory, CPU time, database size, queue depths, integration status, counters - is now taken independently, and a source the server cannot read falls back to a placeholder and names itself, with the reason, in a Degraded readings panel at the top of the Overview page. Previously a single unavailable reading made the entire request fail, which left the dashboard showing nothing but an error and gave no indication which reading was at fault. A diagnostics endpoint that answers with an error tells an operator only that the diagnostics are broken too. No engine behaviour, configuration or database changes.

Orca Observatory now has its own address. Instead of living inside the Jellyfin admin interface, the dashboard is served by the plugin at http://<your-server>/OrcaEngine/Observatory/App - still the same Jellyfin server, the same port and the same process, just a page of its own rather than one injected into Jellyfin's dashboard. Because it no longer runs inside Jellyfin's web client, it cannot borrow the admin session it used to, so it now signs in against Jellyfin directly: enter your Jellyfin administrator username and password once, and the access token it returns is kept in the browser. Your password is never stored, and the token can be revoked at any time from Dashboard - Devices. Accounts without administrator rights are refused at sign-in rather than being let in to meet a wall of permission errors, and an expired or revoked token drops you back to the sign-in screen instead of leaving a dead page. The Orca Observatory entry has been removed from the Jellyfin sidebar accordingly; the plugin's own settings page is unchanged and still lives under Dashboard - Plugins. Moving out also removes the whole class of faults that came from living inside another application's page loader - the blank dashboard fixed in 1.0.12.1 was one of them. No engine behaviour, configuration or database changes.

Fixes the Orca Observatory dashboard, which rendered as a blank page in 1.0.12.0. The engine serializes its responses with property names exactly as declared, and the dashboard's snapshot reader expected the other capitalisation - so one lookup returned nothing, reading a field from it threw, and React tore the whole page down before anything drew. The dashboard now reads every field from the engine case-insensitively, with defaults for anything absent, so a payload it does not recognise can no longer blank it. Three further hardening changes came out of the same fault: each page is wrapped in an error boundary, so a failure in one panel shows that panel's error and leaves the rest of the dashboard working instead of emptying the screen; the dashboard now waits for the Jellyfin page container to appear rather than assuming it is present the instant its script runs; and the page carries visible placeholder text, so a script that never executes is distinguishable at a glance from one that started and failed. Upgrade directly from 1.0.12.0 - there are no configuration or database changes, and no engine behaviour changes.

Adds Orca Observatory, an observability dashboard for the engine that lives inside the Jellyfin admin interface (Dashboard - Orca Observatory). It answers the questions the server log could not: which home row is the bottleneck, why a TMDB call failed, why a trailer is missing, why a title was recommended, and what the engine is doing right now. Eleven pages cover overview and engine health, per-row performance, metadata, the trailer resolver, the recommendation pipeline with per-pick score breakdowns, cache hit rates, a live log stream with full stack traces, a timeline of engine activity, and users. Behind it, every outbound call to TMDB, Sonarr, Radarr, Jellyseerr and the LLM is now timed and its failures recorded with status codes and exception detail, rather than collapsing into a bare counter; cache hits and misses, background maintenance ticks, and the previously invisible profile recompute backlog are all reported. IMPORTANT - administrative endpoints now require an authenticated Jellyfin administrator and return 403 otherwise. This covers all Admin and Observatory routes, the maintenance operations (catalog resync, reconcile, purge, TMDB and provider enrichment, global discovery pull, sweep, content-warning enrichment, community-rating recompute) and the operator diagnostics (trailer diagnostics, discovery runs and source stats); previously every one of these was reachable anonymously, including the endpoint that wipes all counters. Client-facing routes are unchanged. Also fixes a real defect: the plugin applied a cache size limit to Jellyfin's shared memory cache rather than its own, which could make unrelated server code throw when caching entries without a declared size. The engine now owns a private cache.

The home is now built row by row, concurrently, instead of one row after another. Every row - Continue Watching, Recently Added, For You, Because You Watched, Coming Soon, and the trending and discovery rows - is produced independently under its own time budget, so the page costs the slowest single row rather than the sum of all of them. A row that is slow or fails is simply absent from that build instead of stalling or failing the whole home, and the LLM curation step carries its own tighter budget, so a slow Groq call costs a row its curation but never the row itself. Cached homes are now served instantly and refreshed in the background (stale-while-revalidate: 5 minutes soft, 30 minutes hard) rather than expiring outright, so a viewer rarely waits for a rebuild at all. Together these stop a cold personalized home from taking so long that the Orca X client times out and falls back to its legacy home.

Spotlight showcase cards now carry their title's genuine metadata as structured badges - certificate, community score, premiere year, runtime, and up to three genres - read straight from the catalog record and omitted when a value does not exist. Showcase cards also correctly declare backdrop-led wide artwork (previously they defaulted to poster/tall), so discover titles lead with the right image, and they request inline trailers whenever the client supports them. Pairs with the Orca X client's redesigned Spotlight, which renders these values as a single metadata line.

Adds the cinematic Spotlight showcase: single-title rows rendered nearly full-screen in the Orca X home, which play that title's trailer inline once focused. These are separate from the rotating billboard at the top of the home - several appear per home, placed deep in the feed among the library and discovery rows rather than stacked under the billboard, and only titles with backdrop artwork are chosen. Controlled by a new 'Spotlight showcase' feature toggle and count (default 2), independent of the existing billboard spotlight settings. Requires an Orca X client build that advertises the Spotlight card type; older clients simply do not receive the rows.

Fixes AI features silently falling back during the first minutes after a restart: the discovery cycle used to fire every viewer's LLM and embedding calls back-to-back, which could exceed a provider's rate limit and make every call fail with no retry. LLM (Groq, OpenAI, etc.) and embedding (Voyage, Jina, OpenAI) calls now recognize a rate-limit response and retry once after the wait the provider asks for, capped to 10 seconds - a brief burst now recovers instead of degrading the whole cycle to local-only ranking.

AI curation of every personalized surface (opt-in 'Enable AI curation of personalized rows'): the LLM now genuinely selects the For You row and Spotlight from a wide locally-ranked pool (instead of only re-ordering the top picks), curates the daily mood collections so each row only contains titles that truly carry the mood, picks the More Like This titles a fan of the source would actually reach for, and orders Coming Soon by how much each viewer will care (state logic still decides what appears - nothing airs unseen). List rows - trending, popular in your country, recently added - stay algorithmic by design. Every surface degrades to the built-in local ranking if the model is unavailable, and results are cached per surface to keep API usage small. Works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint configured in the AI section.

Optional AI recommendations: connect any OpenAI-compatible model - Groq, OpenAI, a local Ollama server, OpenRouter and others - and the engine asks it to suggest new titles from each viewer's own watch history. Those become the You Might Like and Because You Watched picks, each with a short reason. It weighs what you loved, finished and disliked along with your favourite genres and people, and only surfaces a pick after confirming the title exists on TMDB. If the model is unavailable or a viewer's taste isn't established yet, it falls back to the built-in TMDB discovery automatically, and it only fills home rows - it never requests or downloads anything by itself. The AI settings now accept any OpenAI-compatible base URL, key and model; existing Groq keys keep working unchanged. Trailers can now prefer a chosen audio language, falling back to the title's native trailer.

Smarter home rows driven by what you actually watch, not the raw download schedule. 'New Since You Were Away' now shows only genuine events - a movie that became available, or a series whose episode aired or downloaded while you were gone - and never mislabels an old unwatched season as new. New 'Continue the Story' row surfaces shows you started but didn't finish: seasons you skipped and series you abandoned (kept separate from Continue Watching, so a show appears in just one card). Coming Soon is now personalized: your monitored series lead with their next episode, new seasons of shows you've watched are highlighted, and the rest is filtered to high-quality, taste-matched upcoming titles instead of the whole calendar. No new database tables; the home degrades gracefully if Sonarr/Radarr is unreachable.

Trailer previews rebuilt for instant, reliable playback. Trailers now have an explicit lifecycle with a queryable status instead of the app guessing from repeated 404s. A single priority queue with a small bounded worker pool produces them highest-priority-first and can no longer swamp the server with parallel yt-dlp/ffmpeg jobs. Warming is now predictive - Continue Watching, what you've recently focused and played, your interest history, popularity and time of day - rather than just top-rated titles. A new cache manager keeps disk usage bounded (evicts least-used, pins frequently-viewed, expires stale, verifies files). Adds priority-aware prefetch, a smarter preview start offset, and a /Trailer/Diagnostics endpoint. Backward compatible; adds additive trailer-state tables (schema v9/v10).

Fixes a home-screen error (no cards) that could occur when Taste-driven discovery was enabled: the 'What people are watching in your country' row built a database query that could not be translated to SQL. Home row providers now also fail safe, so one broken row can never blank the whole home. (1.0.5.0 added taste-driven discovery, per-user taste profiles, recommendation memory, self-explaining For You, richer taste signals, household time zone, retention, and /Admin/Diagnostics.)

Taste-driven discovery (opt-in): the engine pulls TMDB titles matched to each viewer instead of importing blindly - every external title on the home screen now has a traceable reason. New rows: You Might Like, Because You Watched X, Trending with a pinch of your taste, and What people are watching in your country. Adds a per-user taste profile, recommendation memory (stops re-surfacing titles you keep ignoring, with a cooldown that heals over time), and controlled exploration. For You is self-explaining even without an LLM. Richer taste signals: runtime length, maturity, language and franchise. Time-of-day recommendations now honor a configurable household time zone. Operational: behavior-event retention with bounded recompute, a bounded cache, and a new /Admin/Diagnostics endpoint. Enable it in the plugin settings (Taste-driven discovery) with a TMDB key; off by default.

Full-length trailers (no more 60s cut, better source quality); trailer warming is now a real Jellyfin scheduled task (Dashboard > Scheduled Tasks, default every 60h, trigger user-editable); genuine LLM Because You Watched picks (Groq) with why-blurbs when configured; the '... to Request' rows are folded back into a single Worth Requesting row; the plugin now reports its real version (assembly version was stuck at 1.0.0.0).

Trailer cache now pre-warms requestable (discover) titles too - the 16:9 rows that actually play inline trailers - with more titles per cycle (24+24 every 2h, was 12 WatchNow-only every 6h; per-batch cap raised 15 to 60). The manual Prebuffer endpoint covers both pools and accepts up to 60 titles.

LAN app-update channel: the engine mirrors the newest Orca X GitHub release (Update/Latest) and disk-caches its APKs (Update/Apk), so TV clients check for updates against the server and download the APK over the LAN instead of from GitHub every time.

Fix the plugin dashboard Status and Operations panel: the config page was calling the old WholphinEngine routes after the OrcaEngine rename, so status showed as unavailable and the operation buttons were dead.

First alpha: personalized home (spotlight, For You, Because You Watched, mood rows), behavior capture and affinity profiles, content recommender with diversity re-rank, availability-aware Jellyseerr discovery and engine-proxied requests, cross-row de-duplication and expanded requestable rows.
